Extraction: Enhancing Control Room Operator Decision Making
Joseph Mietkiewicz; Ammar N. Abbas; Chidera W. Amazu; Gabriele Baldissone; Anders L. Madsen; Micaela Demichela; Maria Chiara Leva

Control room operators in industrial (chemical) plants are inundated with tasks and alerts, leading to task overload, decision fatigue and reliance on cognitive biases that compromise decision making during critical process disturbances; DSSs for such safety-critical settings must be effective yet interpretable and trustworthy (Abstract, p. 1; Sec. 1, p. 2). Note: the problem domain is industrial process control, not IT operations/SRE.

AI-based DSS framework called "Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence for Safety-Critical Systems" (HAISC): a dynamic influence diagram (DID; Bayesian-network-based, built in HUGIN software from expert knowledge and physical process equations) detects anomalies via conflict analysis, forecasts states over 10 one-minute time slices and recommends maximum-expected-utility actions; localized deep RL agents (TD3-based, in a multi-specialized reinforcement learning agent (M-SRLA) setup where multiple agents run independently and a specific agent is activated when the DID detects an abnormality) refine interval recommendations into precise continuous values, accepted only if inside the DID-recommended interval — otherwise the interpretable DID suggestion takes precedence; the model operates within a human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework assisting, not replacing, the operator (Sec. 3.2, p. 18; Algorithm 1, p. 19; Sec. 3.1.5, p. 17).

Controlled between-subjects experiment in a simulated formaldehyde-production control room (production of 10,000 kg/h of 30% formaldehyde solution; 80 alarms of different priority levels incl. nuisance alarms; 3 fault scenarios); 48 volunteer participants, predominantly chemical-engineering master's students: Group G1 without DSS n=23, Group G2 with DSS n=25; measures: SART and SPAM for situation awareness, NASA TLX for workload, reaction time / response time / overall performance from operational data (21 participants per group), smartwatch physiological data — heart rate, temperature, EDA (G1 n=14, G2 n=17); statistics: Shapiro–Wilk, Levene's test, Student's/Welch's T-test, Wilcoxon rank-sum / Mann–Whitney U (p < 0.05) (Sec. 2.1, p. 5; Sec. 2.5, p. 13; Sec. 4, pp. 21–26).

Not applicable for MTTD/MTTR as such (industrial control-room study, not IT incident response); analogous time-to-detect/act metrics improved with the DSS: mean reaction time S1 106.96 (G2) vs 276.30 (G1), S2 63.43 vs 266.91, S3 117.38 vs 190.17; mean response time S1 259.04 vs 339.30, S2 154.83 vs 361.48, S3 680.00 vs 787.87 (units not stated in Table 5); Wilcoxon tests show significant differences except in scenario 3 (reaction time p=0.00 S1/S2 vs 0.14 S3; overall performance p=0.00/0.05/1.00); frustration (NASA TLX) significantly lower with DSS (p=0.04/0.02) while overall TLX index showed no significant difference (Sec. 4.4, Tables 4–5, pp. 25–26; Sec. 4.3, Table 3, p. 24).

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: Demonstrates a hierarchical HITL architecture in which multiple specialized RL agents function independently and only the relevant agent is activated upon DID-detected anomaly (M-SRLA); safety guardrail: the black-box RL continuous value is used only if it falls within the interpretable DID's recommended interval (e.g., in scenario 1 the RL agent suggested 5.6 m3/h inside the DID range 4–7 m3/h); trade-off uncovered: the DSS group showed significantly lower situation awareness (SPAM index, monitoring and intervention, p=0.00), attributed to possible over-reliance on the system's guidance, while heart rate was borderline lower with DSS (Welch p=0.05) (Sec. 3.2, p. 18; Sec. 3.3, pp. 19–20; Sec. 4.2, Table 2, pp. 22–23; Sec. 4.5, Table 6, p. 26; Sec. 5.2, p. 29).

Scalability: constructing a DID covering the entire process from physical equations is challenging and time-intensive, forcing focus on parts of the plant or more generic models/recommendations; participants were mostly chemical-engineering students who "lack real-world experience as control room operators"; physiological data analyzed raw, without accounting for individual differences; DID discretization trades precision against unwieldy CPT size and high computational time; future work: optimize discretization and model complexity, revise CPTs (including integrating empirical data), and add a "What If" display of consequences of recommended actions (Sec. 5.1, pp. 28–29; Sec. 5.3, pp. 29–30).

Although set in an industrial control room rather than IT operations, this paper empirically validates the exact HITL pattern my thesis proposes: an AI copilot that detects anomalies and recommends actions while the human operator keeps decision authority. Its evidence that AI decision support significantly cuts reaction and response times to faults parallels the MTTD/MTTR reductions I target in incident response, and the reduced frustration and heart rate speak directly to alert fatigue and operator cognitive load. The measured trade-off — lower situation awareness from over-reliance on the system — is a key design caution for an incident-response copilot that must keep the on-call engineer engaged. Finally, its guardrail pattern (black-box RL output accepted only within an interpretable model's safe interval) is transferable to safe agentic automation in production environments.

Medium — adjacent: it empirically measures human-in-the-loop AI decision support with time-to-react/respond gains and cognitive-workload effects, but in industrial process control rather than IT incident response, and it does not report MTTD/MTTR.
